    Semi-join reduction
    
      
    
        
    node
    a relation; the edges are the joins of the query, a tree with root R
    
        
    boxes
    the keys and join attributes of a relation: a row per tuple, a column per attribute
    
        
    colour
    a key: a blue, b orange, c violet; equal colours mean equal keys
    
        
    key column
    the keys a relation sends, one box per key; at the other relation they are drawn out
          beside its rows, an empty frame beside a row whose key is not among them
    
        
    X  Y
    the semi-join of X with Y, i.e., the rows of X whose key is also in Y
    
        
    dark row
    gone: its key is not in the other relation
    
        
    ′ ″ ′′′
    a relation after one, two or three semi-joins
    
        
    green
    the rows left after both passes: exactly those that take part in the join
    
      
    
      
    Yannakakis, VLDB 1981. Lecture 04b (slides 34–44) and the ResultDB
        paper (Nix and Dittrich, Extending SQL to Return a Subdatabase, SIGMOD 2025) use it to compute a subdatabase;
        the notebook
        Result-DB.ipynb computes the same reduction on an example of
        its own. The data here is invented.
